newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria Socialists agree wider powers for cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria Socialists agree wider powers for cabinet.

text.p: Bulgaria's outgoing Socialist rulers agreed on Tuesday to give a caretaker cabinet powers to negotiate and conclude agreements with international lenders to alleviate the country's severe economic crisis.
"We gave our support for the actions of the president and of a future caretaker government," Socialist leader Georgi Parvanov told reporters.
"Some consider our decision to be the end of the political crisis, but we think it is the first step."

Leaders of all political parties in parliament agreed on Monday that the interim cabinet must speed up long-delayed structural reforms, such as boosting privatisation, closing loss-making state firms, cracking down on corruption and the grey economy, and encouraging investment.

They met again on Tuesday to discuss the powers of the interim cabinet and to sign the final document. The Socialists, who have the majority in the outgoing parliament, had previously opposed giving a caretaker cabinet wider powers.
The Socialists agreed last week after 30 days of nationwide protests to give up trying to form a cabinet.
President Petar Stoyanov is expected to appoint a caretaker cabinet on Wednesday under Sofia mayor Stefan Sofianski to govern until after elections in mid-April.
Parliament will meet on Wednesday to approve Tuesday's decision, which would give the interim cabinet powers to seek credits for grain imports and to negotiate with the International Monetary Fund.
The session will also discuss amendments to the electoral law and income tax law.
As the political parties met, about 300 army officers gathered outside the presidency for a second day to protest over their pay increases.

Officers at the Georgi Rakovski military academy in Sofia spent Monday sitting in the film hall as a sign of protest after their pay was increased by 60 percent last week while other state salaries were doubled.
Outgoing defence minister Dimitar Pavlov told reporters he would ask the cabinet to bring their wage rise in line with the rest of the state sector.

Inflation has soared as the national currency has collapsed and the main Confederation of Independent Trade Unions says 61,882 levs is needed to feed one person for a month, compared to 18,311 levs in January.
Chief prosecutor Ivan Tatarchev met Stoyanov on Monday and expressed concern about capital flight out of the country.

"The president believes the nation's wealth has been exported in the last few days, and my opinion is that this has been going on ever since the Bulgarian Socialist Party came to power," Tatarchev told reporters.
He promised anyone found guilty would be prosecuted, though local media said at the weekend only 24 people have been jailed for corruption in Bulgaria since 1989.
Konstantin Trenchev, leader of the Podkrepa trade union, said last week $70 million was still leaving Bulgaria every week.
